claims.text: The initial eutectic HEA contains an FCC matrix and fine, interconnected ordered B2 domains.
Intermediate thermal aging promotes LCO evolution and B2-domain coarsening.
The proposed intermediate-aging regime does not cause grain coarsening or impurity segregation.
Intermediate aging causes coarsened B2 ordered domains to form a percolating network.
Intermediate aging increases the density of superlattice intrinsic stacking faults and complex stacking faults within the B2 phase.
LCOs evolve into larger, interconnected B2 regions during intermediate aging.
Dislocations in the FCC matrix must cut through or bypass the ordered B2 domains.
Shearing ordered B2 domains requires high energy because it creates SISFs or CSFs.
A percolating B2 network creates a continuous network of high Peierls barriers.
The high barriers associated with the percolating B2 network severely impede dislocation motion and cause brittleness.
At higher aging temperatures, long-range B2 order decreases or chemically disordered phase-boundary layers form.
Disordering at higher temperatures lowers the barrier to dislocation motion.
The lower barrier permits dislocations to bypass or shear B2 domains more easily and restores ductility.
Elongation to failure will show a sharp minimum where the B2 network is maximally continuous and ordered.
Ductility will recover when the order parameter decreases or disorder disrupts network connectivity.
The embrittlement regime begins when B2-domain connectivity exceeds a critical percolation threshold for dislocation blocking.
The embrittlement regime ends before significant disordering or phase decomposition occurs.
Easy dislocation glide through B2 domains without SISF or CSF creation would falsify the proposed mechanism.
A ductility minimum that correlates with grain-boundary segregation rather than B2-domain percolation would falsify the hypothesis.
